h: Fish Quays, Lighthouses and Spanish City Sparkle
p: Tynemouth Aquarium makes a brilliant anchor for a whole day on the coast, and the trick is to time it with the weather. If the morning dawns grey and drizzly, head inside first and save the beach for when the clouds clear. If it's glorious, do the sands and the headland first, then duck into the aquarium when little legs need a rest or the sea breeze gets a bit too bracing.

Inside, catch any talks or feeding times you can, as these are often when the animals are at their liveliest and the staff share the best facts. Younger kids tend to be happiest with plenty of time at the tunnel tank, so don't rush them through.

Tynemouth has more up its sleeve once you're back outside. Look out for the towering Collingwood Monument, honouring Admiral Lord Collingwood, Nelson's second-in-command at Trafalgar, which overlooks the mouth of the Tyne. King Edward's Bay, a sheltered sandy cove tucked below the priory, is a gorgeous spot for a paddle. At weekends, Tynemouth Market fills the old Victorian station with stalls selling food, antiques and crafts.

Walk along the river to North Shields and you'll reach the Fish Quay, packed with fishmongers and chippies serving fish that's barely left the boat. Up the coast, Whitley Bay's restored Spanish City dome has food and drink, and St Mary's Lighthouse sits on a tidal island you can walk out to when the tide allows.
Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay all sit on the Metro, so you can hop between them without worrying about parking.
